newsitem.title: UK: UK's Brown calls on companies to help jobs crusade.
newsitem.headline: UK's Brown calls on companies to help jobs crusade.

text.p: British finance minister Gordon Brown called on private sector companies on Tuesday to join the government in what he called a "national crusade" to get unemployed youngsters into jobs.
Brown, Chancellor of the Exchequer since the Labour Party's landslide May 1 election victory, said there were 400,000 young people out of work.
In some of Britain's poorest communities one third of all young people were doing nothing and in some of these places unemployed youngsters were the children of unemployed parents.

"I think we recognise that public and private sectors must work together to address problems that, if not tackled together, we may not tackle successfully at all," Brown said in a speech to businessmen.
Brown has made getting the young back to work a centrepiece of Labour's economic policy.
He said the government planned four options for every young person, each involving training that would lead to qualifications.
These were: a job with an employer, work with a voluntary organisation, work with an environmental task force and, for those without basic qualifications, full time education or training.
"There will be no fifth option -- to stay at home doing nothing," Brown said.
He said the four options were an essential part of recently announced government plans to reform the system of welfare benefits, by making the unemployed employable.
"So we expect training will account for about a third of our welfare-to-work programme," Brown said.
He said the government wanted to build on existing successes in the field of youth employment.
He singled out The Prince's Trust, an organisation set up by heir-to-the-throne Prince Charles, who was present to hear Brown speak, to help young people in the world of work.
Brown praised "success like the Prince's Trust volunteers who since 1991 have helped 16,000 young people to prepare for work. Eighty percent of them find a job within a year.
"By the year 2000 they plan to have a throughput of 25,000 young people every year.

"Our goal is not just to take people off the streets for six months, but to make the unemployed employable and to rebuild the welfare state away from the benefits culture and now around the work ethos," said Brown.

"I want you all to feel part of what I regard as a national crusade to tackle once and for all the threat of an underclass in our country, to address a problem which we all know must be addressed, to rebuild a strong cohesive society on which in the long term a strong economy depends."
